## Computational Photography

## Modèle d'imagerie

### Photographie conventionnelle

Dans la photographie conventionnelle, le pipeline est simple et linéaire :

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Monde réel] --> B[Optique]
    B --> C[Image capturée]
    C --> D[Calcul]
    D --> E[Image améliorée]
```

- L'**optique** capture quelque chose de proche de l'image finale
- Le **calcul** sert principalement à *améliorer* l'image capturée (ex. : deblurring)

### Photographie computationnelle

La photographie computationnelle généralise ce pipeline :

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Monde réel] --> B[Optique généralisée]
    B --> C[Représentation codée]
    C --> D[Calcul généralisé]
    D --> E[Image(s) finales]
```

- L'**optique généralisée** encode le monde dans une représentation intermédiaire
- Le **calcul généralisé** décode cette représentation en une ou plusieurs images

> **Idée clé** : we shift the complexity from optics to calculation, thus gaining flexibility.

### Paramètres optiques contrôlables

Les paramètres d'un système optique sur lesquels on peut agir :

- Ouverture (*aperture*)
- Profondeur de champ (*depth of field*)
- Champ de vue (*field of view*)
- Exposition (*exposure*)
- Bruit (*noise*)
- Tableaux de filtres couleur (*color filter arrays*, CFA)

---

## Founding example: the CFA mosaic (*mosaicing*)

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Monde réel] --> B["Optique généralisée\n(CFA)"]
    B --> C["Représentation codée\n(mosaïque)"]
    C --> D["Calcul généralisé\n(dématriçage)"]
    D --> E["Image finale\n(RGB)"]
```

- The **Color Filter Array (CFA)** encodes color in mosaic form
- **Demosaicing*** decodes this mosaic into a complete RGB image

---

## Pinhole Camera (*Pinhole Camera*)

**Principle**: an infinitely small aperture replaces the lens.

- ✅ Everything is sharp (infinite depth of field)
- ❌ Very inefficient in terms of light captured

---

## Lens Camera (*Lens Camera*)

**Principle**: a lens replaces the pinhole to collect more light.

- ✅ Very efficient in terms of light
- ❌ Only one shot is in focus at a time → **focus problem**

> **Question**: How to obtain a completely sharp image?

---

## Focal Stack (*Focal Stack*)

### Concept

**Analogy** with HDR seen previously:

| HDR | FocalStack |
|---|---|
| Stack images at different exposures | Stack images focused on different planes |
| Merge into an HDR image | Merge into a fully sharp image |

### Capture procedure

To capture a focal stack:

1. Take multiple images focused on different **depth planes**
2. Merge into one fully sharp image (*all-in-focus*)

**Parameter to modify**: we turn the **focus ring** (and not the zoom!), which changes the **lens-sensor distance $D'$**.

#### Lens conjugation law

$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{D} + \frac{1}{D'}$$

with :

- $f$: focal length of the lens
- $D$: lens-object distance
- $D'$: lens-sensor distance

### Focal Stack Merge

#### Step 1: Aligning Images

**Why align?** When you change the focusing distance, you also change the **magnification** (field of view), which causes a slight zoom between images.

Assuming that $f$ and all the values ​​of $D'$ are known, we can correct this change in magnification by **resizing** (*resize*) according to the conjugation equations.

#### Step 2: Assigning weights

For each pixel, we measure its **local sharpness** in order to know if it is well in focus:

1. Apply the **Laplacian operator** (edge ​​detector → sharp areas)
2. Apply a **Gaussian blur** to regularize

→ The stronger the response, the sharper the pixel.

#### Step 3: Weighted Merge

$$I_{\text{fused}}(x,y) = \frac{\sum_k w_k(x,y) \cdot I_k(x,y)}{\sum_k w_k(x,y)}$$

with $w_k(x,y)$ the sharpness weight of pixel $(x,y)$ in image $k$.

---

## Advanced depth techniques

### Confocal Stereo (*Confocal Stereo*)

*[Hassinoff and Kutulakos, ECCV 2006]*

- Captures a **2D stack** by varying both focus **and** aperture
- Analyzes the focal-aperture image of each pixel to estimate **actual depth**
- ✅ Estimate per pixel

### Depth by defocus (*Depth from Defocus*)

*[Shree K. Nayar]*

- Uses only **two images** with different defocuses
- Blur kernels: $h_{z_1}(x,y)$ and $h_{z_2}(x,y)$ for images $G_1(x,y)$ and $G_2(x,y)$
- Estimate depth by comparing blur levels
- ✅ Requires few images
- ❌ Estimate per patch (not per pixel)

### Focal Flow (*Focal Flow*)

*[Alexander et al., ECCV 2016; Guo et al., ICCV 2017, PNAS 2019]*

**Biological inspiration**: jumping spiders use this principle!

**Principle**:

1. Use a **dense focal stack** (e.g. from autofocus)
2. Model the circle of confusion as a blur kernel (typically Gaussian) with variable $\sigma$
3. Estimate the **optical flow** between successive images of the stack
4. Link the change in optical flow to **depth**

- ✅ Very little calculation (no convolutions)
- ❌ Only works on textured areas

### Summary of depth techniques

| Technical | Entry required | Granularity |
|---|---|---|
| Depth from focus | Focal Stack | By patch |
| Depth from defocus | 2 images | By patch |
| Confocal stereo | Focal stack + aperture | Per pixel |
| Focal flow | Dense focal stack | Per patch (effective) |

##LightFieldPhotography

## Light field theory

### Motivation

A typical photograph only captures a **fraction** of the light information entering the camera.

A **light field camera*)** additionally captures:

- The direction of origin of each light ray
- How light coming from one part of the lens differs from light coming from another

### Definition of the light field

The light field is defined as the **geometric distribution of light rays** circulating in space.

$$L = L(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)$$

It is a **plenotic function* (*plenoptic function*) with 5 dimensions**:

- $3D$ for each spatial position $(x, y, z)$
- $2D$ for each propagation direction $(\theta, \phi)$

### 5D plenotic function

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    P["Fonction plénotique 5D\nL(x, y, z, θ, φ)"]
    P --> S["Position spatiale\n(x, y, z) — 3D"]
    P --> D["Direction de propagation\n(θ, φ) — 2D"]
```

The **light field** (or *radiance*) completely encodes the state of light at any point in space.

---

## Capturing a light field

### Radius measurement

A light ray can be parameterized by its intersection with **two parallel planes**:

- $st$ plane (at lens level)
- $uv$ plane (at sensor level)

> **Key property**: The same set of rays can be captured by a **moving pinhole camera** from multiple viewpoints.

### Option 1: Multiple camera array

*[Wilburn et al., SIGGRAPH 2005]*

- **Stanford Camera Array** → *"synthetic aperture"*
- ✅ High spatial and angular resolution
- ❌ Bulky and expensive

### Option 2: Moving a single camera

- Single camera mounted on a motor (e.g. LEGO)
- Take multiple images from different positions
- ❌ Scene must be **static**

### Option 3: Plenoptic Camera (*Plenoptic Camera*)

> **Etymology**: *plenus* (Latin, “full”) + *optic* (Greek, “see”)

First conceptualized by **Gabriel Lippmann** (over a century ago) as *integral photography*.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Monde réel] --> B["Optique généralisée\n(caméra plénoptique)"]
    B --> C["Représentation codée\n(champ lumineux)"]
    C --> D["Calcul généralisé\n(rendu du champ lumineux)"]
    D --> E["Images refocalisées\nou multi-points de vue"]
```

---

## Conventional camera vs light field camera

### Comparative structure

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Caméra conventionnelle"
        L1[Lentille principale] --> S1[Capteur]
    end
    subgraph "Caméra plénoptique"
        L2[Lentille principale] --> MLA[Tableau de microlentilles]
        MLA --> S2[Capteur]
    end
```

The fundamental difference: a **microlens array*** is inserted between the main lens and the sensor.

### Setting up plans

- Plan $st$: plane of the main lens
- $uv$ plane: sensor plane

Each microlens captures rays coming from a small region of the $st$ plane, providing access to the **direction** of the rays.

---

## Numerical operations on the light field

### Digitally stopping-down

- **Principle**: add only the central part of each microlens
- → Simulates a smaller aperture → greater depth of field

### Virtual movement of the observer

- **Principle**: move the extraction window through the microlenses
- → Simulates a change of point of view

### Digital refocusing (*Digital refocusing*)

- **Principle**: add windows extracted from several microlenses with offset
- → Simulates focusing on a different plane *after capture*

> **Major advantage**: you can choose the focus plane **after** having taken the photo!

---

## Lytro Camera

### Presentation

*Lytro* and *Lytro Illum Pro*: first plenoptic cameras for the general public.

### What is the Lytro camera?

- Plenoptic camera with:
  - A photographic **main lens**
  - A **microlens array** (*lens array*)
  - A **digital sensor** (*digital photosensor*)
- Captures the light field to allow **refocusing after the fact**

### Internal components

- **Lens Array**: microlens array
- **Light Field Sensor**: light field sensor
- **Light Field Engine**: light field processing engine
- **Marvell Avastar 88W8787 SoC**: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip

#### Light Field Sensor (*Light Field Sensor*)

- **CMOS sensor**: converts light into electrons → digital values ​​per cell
- **Microlens array**: divides CMOS pixels into zones, showing the image from different angles

#### Lytro Sensor Specifications

- **4000 × 4000 pixels** in total
- **292 × 292 microlenses** (296 according to mechanical specs, ~$37$ mm active area)
- **14 × 14 pixels** per microlens
- $125\ \mu m$ square microlenses
- $0.5mm separation between components

### Industrial plenoptic cameras

Plenoptic cameras have become popular in laboratory and industry:

- ✅ Spatial and angular resolution much higher than consumer cameras
- ✅ Interchangeable lenses
- ✅ Video possible
- ❌ Very expensive

### Advantages and disadvantages of Lytro

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| Very portable | Reduced total resolution |
| Refocusing ability | Fixed opening |

## Conventional camera with coded aperture

## Goals

From a **single input image**, obtain:

1. **Output #1**: a **depth map*
2. **Output #2**: an **all-focused image***

---

## Lens and defocus

### Source point in focus

When a source point is on the **focal plane**:

- All rays converge towards a **single point** on the sensor
- The **Point Spread Function* (PSF)** is a Dirac pulse

### Defocused source point

When the source point is **outside the focal plane**:

- The rays no longer converge → form a **circle of confusion*)**
- The PSF is a **circular disk** whose radius depends on the depth

$$r_{\text{coc}} \propto \left| \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{D} - \frac{1}{D'} \right|$$

---

## Depth by defocus

**Idea**: the radius of the circle of confusion depends on the depth:

$$C_D = \frac{A \cdot f \cdot |D' - D_f|}{D_f \cdot (D' - f)}$$

with :

- $A$: opening diameter
- $D_f$: focusing distance
- $D'$: lens-sensor distance

→ Analyze the **defocus blur scale** to estimate the depth.

---

## Challenges of deconvolution

### Problem 1: Difficult deconvolution even if the kernel is known

- Classic **Richardson-Lucy** algorithm → **severe ringing artifacts**

### Problem 2: Poorly posed deconvolution

The observed image $y$ is linked to the clear image $x$ by:

$$y = f \otimes x + \text{bruit}$$

This inversion is **ill-posed**: there are an infinite number of $x$ solutions compatible with $y$.

---

## Proposed solutions

### Solution 1: Prioritize natural images

**Observation**: natural images have **sparse gradients*.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    N[Images naturelles] --> |"gradients épars"| G[Histogramme en pic]
    U[Images non naturelles] --> |"gradients étalés"| H[Histogramme aplati]
```

**Idea**: impose a **penalty on gradients** during deconvolution.

#### Formulation of deconvolution with prior

$$\hat{x} = \arg\min_x \| f \otimes x - y \|^2 + \lambda \cdot P(\nabla x)$$

with :

- $\| f \otimes x - y \|^2$: **convolution error** (fidelity to the data)
- $P(\nabla x)$: **priority on derivatives** (regularization)
- $\lambda$: compromise parameter

#### Comparison of priors

| Algorithm | Prior $P$ | Behavior | Quality |
|---|---|---|---|
| Richardson-Lucy | none | — | Strong ring |
| Gaussian Prior | $\|\nabla x\|^2$ | Spread the gradients | Medium |
| Prior scattered | $\|\nabla x\|$ | Locates gradients | Best |

---

### Solution 2: Coded Aperture (*Coded Aperture*)

#### Principle

Place a **mask (*code*)** in the lens opening plane:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Ouverture conventionnelle\n(disque plein)"] --> |"remplacée par"| B["Ouverture codée\n(masque binaire)"]
```

**Goal**: make defocus patterns **different from natural images** → easier to discriminate.

#### Why code?

**Frequency problem**: spatial convolution corresponds to frequency multiplication.

$$Y(u,v) = F(u,v) \cdot X(u,v)$$

If $F(u,v)$ has **zeroes** (zero frequencies) → irreversible loss of information → impossibility of inverting.

- **Conventional aperture** (disc): frequency spectrum with zeros → difficult deconvolution
- **Coded aperture**: designed to **avoid zeros** in the spectrum → deconvolution possible

#### Optimal filter design

Analytical search for the pattern maximizing the **discrimination between different defocus scales** (KL divergence):

- Take into account the prior on the images
- Respect physical constraints (binary: open/closed)

**Key property**: if the filter has **no frequency zeros** → direct inversion possible.

---

## Pipeline overview with coded opening

### Local defocus pattern

The local window $V'$ of the image is modeled as:

$$V' = f_\lambda \otimes V$$

with $f_\lambda$: blur kernel calibrated to depth $\lambda$.

### Regularized depth estimation

1. Deconvolve with **10 different aperture scales**:
   $$\hat{x}_\lambda = \arg\min_x \| f_\lambda \otimes x - y \|^2 + \lambda \cdot P(\nabla x)$$

2. **Select** the minimum error scale in each local window

3. **Regularize** depth estimation (smoothed depth map)

4. **Deconvolve** with kernel selected → sharp image

### Results obtained

- ✅ Depth map + sharp image from a **single image**
- ✅ **No loss of resolution** compared to conventional camera
- ✅ **Simple modification** of the lens (addition of the mask)
- ⚠️ Coarse depth: impossible on non-textured areas, may require manual corrections
- ⚠️ Slight **loss of light** (mask blocks part)

### Digital refocusing from a single image

Depth estimation makes it possible to simulate **a posteriori refocusing**, similar to the plenoptic camera — but from **a single shot** with a simply modified camera.

---

## Camera with generalized optics

## Motivation

Instead of modifying the **aperture**, we can directly modify the **optics** (the lens itself).

$$\text{Distance objet } D \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Distance focale } D'$$

---

## Wavefront Coding (*Wavefront Coding*)

### Principle

Replace the lens with a Cubic Phase Plate.

- **Standard lens**: the rays converge towards the focal plane → PSF very different depending on the depth
- **Wavefront coding**: the rays no longer converge exactly → PSF **approximately invariant in depth** over a given range

### Advantage

$$\text{PSF}(x,y,D) \approx \text{PSF}(x,y) \quad \text{pour } D \in [D_{\min}, D_{\max}]$$

→ A **single deconvolution** is sufficient for any deblurrer, whatever the depth.

---

## Lattice Lens (*Lattice Lens*)

### Principle

Add a **lenslet array* in front of the main lens.

→ Looks like a plenoptic camera (see Lytro microlens table)

### Spectral properties

- Light field spectrum: **4D**
- Image spectrum: **2D**
- Depth: **1D**

→ Only the **3D variety** corresponding to the physical focus distance is useful.

$$\dim(\text{utile}) = 3 \quad \text{sur } 4D \text{ total}$$

**Consequence**: the PSF is **not** depth invariant → local deconvolution necessary (as for the coded aperture).

---

## Comparison of approaches

| Approach | Edit | PSF invariance | Depth of field |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard lens | none | No | Low |
| Coded opening | mask in opening | No | Scope |
| Focal sweep | continuous scanning | Partial | Very extensive |
| Wavefront coding | cubic phase plate | **Yes** (approx.) | Scope |
| Lattice lens | lens network | No | Scope |

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Lentille standard] --> B[Ouverture codée]
    B --> C[Focal sweep]
    C --> D[Wavefront coding]
    D --> E[Lattice lens]
    style A fill:#ffcccc
    style E fill:#ccffcc
```
